utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours -- apologies, good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we begin in the usual manner by taking the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of short preliminary matters. First is we asked Your Honours last -- the week before last if we could have an alteration of the dates of the safe conduct. We haven't had that yet. If we don't get it today, we won't get the witness here for the specified period. So if I can point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have been alerted to that problem, and as soon as the order -- the -- the latest thing is that the form -- it is being formalised, and we will -- it will be issued today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in addition, we asked for witness summonses for ST-179 and ST-123; the dates of their testimony are a couple of weeks or so hence. Again, if we don't get those urgently, we're not likely to get the witnesses to court. I don't say today, but for not very much delay. Your Honours, additionally, Your Honours, I believe on the last Friday we sat, asked us to file something today in relation to the site visit. We won't be able to. We considered Your Honours had a fair bit to get on with in any event. But there was a slight misunderstanding. We were going to discuss it with the Defence so we could come to an agreed list of sites. Obviously the Defence were not here last week. They thought we were going to provide a list and then they'd comment on it. Well, we haven't done it. And so I'm afraid that will have to wait for a little bit while we hopefully get together and discuss that this week. Your Honour, that's the third thing. The fourth thing is in relation to exhumations. We said we would file the database to be added to our 65 ter list. When we get a check, of course, we discovered it was already on our 65 ter list. The various components of this database are 65 ter numbers - I have written them down somewhere - yes, 2517 to 2568. It is our intention purely to produce the database without calling any evidence, and it's a matter for the Defence to say whether they want evidence called from the compilers of the database. And, Your Honours, I think that concludes all the preliminary matters which I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is reminded in respect of -- that in respect of Ms. Korner's issue about the subpoenas that we still await the responses from the Defence, so the Chamber would need expedited responses in order to go on to the next step. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... no objection. I wonder if we could have an oral -- perhaps just an oral indication later today, after the very first break, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will provide an oral indication later today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So is the Prosecution ready to proceed with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, sir. Good afternoon to you, sir. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Nedjo Vlaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th of May, 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a criminologist. I have a degree in criminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before the Tribunal or in the region in relation to these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- you would appreciate that you have been called as a witness in this matter before the Tribunal which has been appointed to deal with crimes that would have occurred in the former Yugoslavia. The first thing that would have happened is that you would have been invited to make a solemn declaration, the effect of which is that your testimony is on oath. The procedure that is followed is fairly standard for courtrooms, in that the side that is calling you - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions. And then the -- counsel for each of the two accused persons would, if they wish, also have questions of you, and the Prosecution would then have a right to re-examine you on matters arising out of your cross-examination. And after that, the Chamber itself may have questions of you. Do you understand what I have just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, can we start by just looking at your dealings with the Prosecution and Defence in this case. Is it right that you were interviewed in Banja Luka in June of last year?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were told that, because of your position you had the right not to answer questions and the right to have a lawyer present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were prepared to answer the questions and didn't have a lawyer present. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I very gladly testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you just explain in which capacity this witness was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was interviewed as someone who, had this Tribunal been issuing indictments, would have come under the definition of a suspect. Of course, that cannot apply anymore because the Tribunal cannot issue indictments, but people such as Mr. Vlaski are given their rights because of the possibility of prosecution in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you had a chance, didn't you, yesterday, to review the -- the recorded interviews; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think what you said about it was that although you might have expressed certain things differently, the interview did record what you wanted to say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I would have had more to say than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Again -- yes, that's fair enough, Mr. Vlaski. You were told there were time constraints, as there are today, yes. And I think, this morning, were you able to have a period of time with Mr. Zecevic before coming into court to testify?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vlaski. Can we now move, please, to the various positions that you have held. Did you start working for the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the -- in the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The 1st of June, 1974, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, at that stage, were you working in the City Secretariat in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: After completing secondary police school, I was assigned as -- I was assigned to the City Secretariat for the police to general police duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At a late date, however, did you transfer to the state security division?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That is correct. From the 1st of June, 1975, I began to work in the State Security Service, at the Republican Secretariat of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in which area of the State Security Service did you work?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I worked at the state security centre in charge of the Sarajevo area. I worked at the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you, however, in the 1980s, transfer into -- or did you become inspector for the security of persons and facilities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: This was just a regular distribution of posts. As one acquired a certain amount of experience and conditions for promotions, I then was given a different position, and I was assigned to duties of a personal and building security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you still in that position at the time of the multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: After this post, where I carried out these tasks and assignments, I was assigned as an inspector at the -- for the combatting of internal enemies, as this was called. These were assignments that had to do with combatting specifically Serbian nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to have a look in a little more detail there what happened to you after the multi-party elections and particularly in 1991. But after the split in the MUP, were you, for at least a short period of time, in 1992, the -- an under-secretary -- assistant under-secretary, I'm sorry, in the National Security Service under Mr. Skipina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Before I respond to this question, there is one period that is particularly important for this Tribunal and for this testimony, so I wouldn't wish to skip over that. May I speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Before the multi-party elections, I worked at these assignments, counter-nationalist activities, and there was a climate created in Bosnia and Herzegovina already that the police should be depoliticised because change of the political system was expected. It was -- what was being expected was a multi-party system, to this process was proceeding more or less regularly. After the multi-party elections, it was clear that the nationalist parties would win, and all of those patients of ours, or clients, as we used to call them, members from the different ethnic groups that we were covering were now in a position to take over power. This was particularly relevant in the case of Alija Izetbegovic who had been sentenced for Muslim nationalist or fundamentalist activities, depending on how you view these issues. And it was expected that representatives would come from the ranks of other nationalist parties who did have some problems, because of their previous political activity. We were in a position, in the Security Service, to expect those people to come to power precisely because they had been previously prosecuted for their previous activities, especially persons who had taken part in certain activities and were subject to investigations and so on, so we were expecting a certain degree of retaliation and revenge on the part of those people who were about to come to power. As far as the policies of those nationalist parties, they were aimed at implementing those ethnic objectives which prompted them to form political parties in the first place, and represent the interests of the people that they represented. The division of power was effected in such a way that the rule was divided between the SDA, SDS, and the HDZ. And, by inertia, there was a re-alignment among the ranks in certain structures including the police, certain institutions, state organs, and also bodies at lower levels. It was particularly characteristic to note the relationship to the structures of power of those who had been previously processed for their activities, and a characteristic example would be that of Alija Izetbegovic. He did allow for the possibility that the investigators who had conducted investigations against him to be given another chance at a position in these institutions, but probably in somewhat different roles. This was the case also in Croatia with investigators who had been dealing with such matters in Croatia to continue on these duties but to direct them at the -- at their own peoples -- people. So this attitude had an effect and all the institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including those where I had worked. There was publicity given and an image created for certain politicians. They had gained power. And then it was the duty of those people to avenge, in their future work, and work towards their interests and en the interests of the people they represent. This was not the case in the instance of representatives of the Serb people. They felt no need to rely on the support of these structures. At least that a was my impression. I personally worked on the issues of Serb nationalism and clerical nationalism. I would have been the one to deal with these matters. Not even the higher levels of my structures were involved in these political party activities before the elections, because they feared retaliation. Most of the managerial staff who had been involved in the activities availed themselves of the opportunity to retire early, under favourable benefits, and they left their posts. We remained, who were rather inexperienced in view of the newly arisen political situation, and without any political support. Unlike the representatives of the Bosniak and Muslim and Croat people who had absolute political support and an obligation, based on what I was saying earlier on, to repay the debt to these people and to rehabilitate themselves, in a way. Thus, the mandate of setting up the Security Service within the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina was given precisely to Munir Alibabic, the investigator who, at one point, investigated Alija Izetbegovic. According to the information we had, we had contacted Izetbegovic at the time when he was serving his sentence in Foca. It was our expectation that this would have an impact on -- in terms of pacifying someone who had already been convicted of nationalism. However, what happened, in fact, was quite unexpected. The investigator in respect of whom managers grew concerned was completely indifferent to the situation. I personally asked him if he was afraid of how the new structures that came to power may react. His response was, I am a professional, and I fear no one. Thereafter, following the elections, the various structures of power came to be manned based on the agreement reached among the various winning political parties. Since Bosnia-Herzegovina operated on the principle of an agreement among the three peoples, and this principle has, in fact, been built in the law and still exists in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, the agreement on the separation of power proved to be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, can I say this: I'm not proposing to ignore with you the -- the events of 1990 and 1991 and the parliament and the agreements. We have a limited time, as I explained to you this morning. Can I ask what the point is that you want to make in three sentences, if at all possible?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is this: Since I am here, in order to tell the truth, and I would like to at least point to the reaction that you have to take in order to ascertain the truth, and what I have been telling you so far is part of the truth. This is what I have been through; it is it a rather painful experience that I wish to draw your attention to. I also have personal reasons to do so. I have gone through a great deal of things at the time, and all of them are relevant to piecing together the puzzle an understanding the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why I have been trying to tell this story, if you will allow me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say this, Mr. Vlaski. At the end of your evidence, as the Presiding Judge has pointed out, I have no doubt, if you want to and you feel that events that haven't been covered properly, you wish to say something about, you will be allowed to do that. For the moment, as I explained to you, there is a limited time available to both myself and to the Defence. We would like to ask you questions about what we consider to be relevant. And as I say, if, at the end, you feel there are other matters that you wish to draw to the Courts's attention, I'm sure you will be allowed to do that. So could we just, please, try and sum up what you've just said at rather great length. Pre the multi-party elections, your service maintained intelligence on the leaders of all the nationalist parties. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Only in respect of those for whom there was information and knowledge which made them interesting from the point of view of security. In other words, there were indications that these people might pose a security threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you're saying that after the multi-party elections, it was expected that those of you who had, in fact, engaged in these operations might lose your jobs, but that did not happen. Is that the effect of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So can we -- as I say, I'm going to come back to what happened to you and to the police -- the MUP in 1990 and 1991. But I just want to move ahead to your position after the split. Could you have a look, please, at, on the screen, 65 ter 10138.5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 10138.5. It's the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs. It's page 5 of the -- of the bundle. Do you think we can possibly turn it so that it is a rectangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I'm not mistaken, I believe this document has been exhibited already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, P876, sorry. But anyhow, we've got -- it's on the -- it's the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not just objecting, just for the sake of the transcript, because, I mean, I think it is easier if we call it by exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we possibly get it up the right way around. [Microphone not activated] ... I gather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I gather there is a technical problem again and the thing can't be turned the right way up. We can give Mr. Vlaski a hard copy, but I don't know that the defendants have it or the accused have it. Can we move it so that we can see to the right-hand side of the page as we look at it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, we can see there the under-secretary for the SNB, that's the State Security Service, as it became called, was, first of all, shown is Mr. Skipina. And then he was replaced by Dragan Kijac. And I think you agree that that's correct, isn't it? Can you see, Mr. Vlaski? It's not very easy.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I can see it on my screen, but the time-line is somewhat illogical to me. We have skipped from one stage to a stage -- the causes of which need to be explained, and we skipped them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vlaski, I've just told you. I'm going to go back to all the matters that we discussed in Banja Luka that happened in 1991. I merely want to deal with some of the personalities later on. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Very well. I can answer the questions. But, as I say, it was -- in 1992, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not -- yes, all right. Can we just look at, please, for a moment, these -- the names here, and then we're going to go back to 1991 and 1992. Is it right that after the split in the MUP, Skipina became the head of the SNB, of the under-secretary of the SNB, later replaced by Dragan Kijac? You have to say yes, I'm afraid, otherwise it's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You're then shown, together with Mr. Goran Radovic, as an assistant under-secretary. Now for, I appreciate a short period, but was that right, was that your appointment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I was nominated. However, for some other objective reasons, I was not in a position to perform the duty at all because I was in a hospital undergoing a treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Radovic, first of all, was he somebody that you knew and had worked with before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: But, of course. Goran Radovic worked in the Sarajevo state security centre. He was a junior colleague. He worked there until 1991 when, following the multi-party elections, which was the most sensitive period when new divisions emerged, he became the Deputy Chief of this particular division in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Underneath you shown on this diagram is a gentleman named Dragan Devedlaka. Again, was he somebody you knew?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Of course. He, too, worked in the State Security Service before the war that's to say. He was an inspector. Later on, in the period of the divisions and commotion within the State Security Service and the Ministry of the Interior, he became the deputy under-secretary for state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'm not so concerned with the others, but can I look at the top now for a moment. Mico Stanisic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first get to know him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: As early as during our schooling in the secondary police school we met, since Mico was the first generation to have been trained in this particular schooling centre. I was the second generation. I was a year younger. We met at the time but were not close. Or, rather, I knew of him. Perhaps he didn't know of me. I was his junior. Later on, we did not work on -- on positions that would have anything to do one with another, and so we didn't have a professional relationship. And it was only after the war that we resumed any sort of relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. By 1992, therefore, or 1991, rather, how long had you known Mico Stanisic for, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: As of 1991, which was the crucial year for the resolution of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because -- or, rather, in the absence of an agreement between the three political parties surrounding the division of posts, including those in the State Security Service, that's where the problem lay, because our professional colleagues and partners would not agree to a partnership being set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, I am seriously going to come back to 1991. My question was simply this: How long, by 1991, had you known Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Before 1991, as I said, I didn't have occasion to meet with him, because Mr. Stanisic was not charged with policing work, and we didn't have an opportunity to be in touch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, what year were you in the secondary police school when Mico Stanisic was there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That would have been 1971, 1972, or 1973. We could have spent two years in the same facility attending school since he is my senior by one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, on this diagram and then we'll go back to 1991, Momcilo Mandic, did you also know him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The same applies to him as applied to Mr. Stanisic, because he attended the same school. I had occasion to hear of him, but they were my senior schoolmates, and we were not in touch at the time. Subsequently I would hear of him, and we would come across each other, informally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't need that diagram anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back to what happened after the multi-party elections. First, did you join any political party?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: No. It was the political and social system of the time which required all of us, at least those of us employed on security activities, to be members of the League of Communists. Following change and the dissolution of the League of Communists, we received instructions to the effect that the police was supposed to undergo a depoliticising process. After that, I have never become involved in the work of any political party, and I do not believe that I will ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as far as you were concerned, you told us already in the speech you made at the beginning of this afternoon's session, that Mr. Alibabic was appointed to, in fact, the MUP and the State Security. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely Alija Izetbegovic who gave him the chance to create the security sector in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to others, of course; he didn't do it on his own. But he was one of the professionals who was privy to how the work was done, the methods of work, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you then appointed to a different position by Mr. Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Precisely, because there was this need to maintain equality among the ethnic groups, and this was under the constitution, the laws, and the rules that were in force at the time. The posts, the various positions, had to be divided among them, and this should have been done even before the multi-party elections. I said that my senior colleagues who were eligible to retire, in fact, had already retired by that time and left the sector. There were many vacancies. And in my specific case, I don't know about the other ones, the proposals were given by Munir Alibabic, who was the chief of the State Security Service of Sarajevo, that I be appointed the chief of the 5th Administration which was tasked with providing security of persons and facilities of such interest in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was handed down a decision to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at that time, was Mico Stanisic already the secretary to the Sarajevo SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Not at the time, no. This was a very difficult period during which agreements had to be reached about how certain vital posts within the state security sector were to be divided. If we know that Alija Izetbegovic wanted to take over power and, as a representative of the majority people, he wanted to take up the key positions within the minister of police, the foreign ministry, the Presidency, and he also wanted to take over certain lower level positions which carried a certain weight. This was an objective that they wanted to achieve at any cost. The Serb cadres were in an inferior position because the Serbs simply did not understand what the state was like at the time. They took over the Ministry of Agriculture the Ministry of Finance where they found the treasury empty. The Croats were given the Ministry of Defence and other important positions, and this reflected itself on all the future relations within Bosnia-Herzegovina. These institutions were the forum where a certain influence could have been excerpted in the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... for a moment. You're in the Sarajevo SUP as -- in the 5th Administration; was the deputy minister of the interior, Dr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. It was pursuant to the inter-party agreement that he was appointed there, because it was -- this particular position was accorded to a representative of the Serb people, and he was appointed to the post.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Delimustafic was the minister?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. He was nominated by the Party of Democratic Action for that position. Even though there were certain things in his background that would -- that should have precluded him from taking that position, but the -- this was a political decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who nominated Dr. Zepinic as the minister of the interior? Deputy Minister, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The representatives of the Serb people nominated him, and he came from the ranks of the Ministry of Interior to take up this position. He had the requisite knowledge and professional background to perform the duty. That was the assessment made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally on this, was Branko Kvesic, a Croat, the under-secretary for state security?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, that policy of appointing cadres was a consequence of a certain amounts of lobbying. There were a number of candidates for that position. I know for a fact that one of the candidates was a friend of mine, Jozo Leutar; however, some circles from the Catholic church influenced the party leadership, and he was elected as the under-secretary of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm sorry, Mr. Vlaski, again I'm going have to explain to you. Time is limited. If could you just literally answer the questions as simply as possible. Because the simple question was: Was Mr. Kresic, a Croat, appointed. Whilst you were working in Sarajevo during 1991, was Mr. -- were Mr. Radovic and Mr. Devedlaka also working in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, they worked in Sarajevo. Radovic worked at the State Security Service's centre as an inspector, and Devedlaka worked in my administration, when I was the chief, as an inspector in the 5th Administration for the security of persons and facilities at that time. Later there will be some shifts which were a consequence of some other relationships.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to deal with this, please, really shortly, Mr. Vlaski, until we move to September -- July to September of 1991. Were there arguments within the MUP about the allocation of posts between the three nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: There were no arguments. There was a situation at the professional level of a certain trust and confidence, because up to a little bit before that, we had ideal relationships. This was before the elections. And there was no need for us to disagree, because we considered our jobs as our professional duties. So once we, however, saw that there were certain tendencies backed by certain political concepts and ideas which were being carried out by our institutions and behind the backs of us professionals, we became frustrated and then this created tensions. In the beginning, there was no open opposition. There was a kind of security/intelligence game that was present. But people in these conditions are linked by common problems, not common interests. We had no other interest other than the interest in preserving our personal dignity and professional dignity. And then it was our duty to protect the interests of the people that we represented, because that was how the system had been set up. This system was not set up like that before, but new relationships created it, and then we, in the MUP, the police, and the security centre, were experienced not as professionals but were thought of as Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. We would -- we could have been the best professionals ever; however, that would not have made any difference, because the system had began to become deformed from the inside. And it was deformed by those who created and influenced these decisions. Lower levels had no influence on decision making; this was excerpted only by the higher levels of leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have a look, please. We can trace what happened to you through some of the intercepts which you have had a chance to listen to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have, please, up on the screen, 65 ter 1029. Now, Your Honours, Mr. Vlaski's listened to all the intercepts -- oh, it is P7 -- P719. Sorry, it has already been exhibited -- has listened to all the intercepts. We've provided his voice recognition on these intercepts. He is not on them -- I mean, he's not speaking personally. He can assist us to the content. And so I'm going to ask him whether he recognises the voices but without playing them again, as I did with the last witness. And then ask for those, which he's not a party, whether they can maybe MFI those which are not already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you listened to this conversation and you were able to identify -- to recognise the voice of Mr. Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly, before we look at the part that relates to you, tell us, firstly, when did you first meet Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: This was after the elections. By the nature of my duties when I was the chief of the 5th Administration for the security of persons and facilitates, it was my job to provide security for state officials. And when the political situation became more complex, then we had to provide security for party leaders and even for leading members of the clergy. And that is why I had the need to meet and introduce myself to people for whom we were supposed to provide security. And I know Mr. Karadzic from the time that I was working in the service. And you already know the reason why. And this applies not only to him but to many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we look, please, at the second page in English and -- I don't have the B/C/S. I would think it would be the second page in B/C/S as well. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is seeking information, and the other speaker who you weren't able to recognise, but we say is Mr. Mandic, is telling him about a meeting that happened at Simovic. And Mr. Karadzic says: "And was Vlaski" -- "was Vlaski appointed there last week?" Now, this is the 17th of June. Would it have been about then that you had been appointed to the Sarajevo position?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I have to explain this situation to you like this, because it is not so -- from this conversation you cannot really understand it like that. I was replaced as chief of the administration for the security of persons and facilities, and it was a position that was -- two-way position that in the leadership hierarchy was meaningless, in the national security sector under the pretext that the rules on internal classifications of posts had been changed. A Bosniak, a Muslim, was appointed in my place, and I was not given another assignment. I didn't have a job anymore. And this small irrelevant position in the hierarchy bothered somebody because it was occupied by somebody who was a member of the Serbian people. From the professional point of view, it was irrelevant, which ethnic group was given that particular job. The entire leadership structure in the national security station was divided by the SDA and the HDZ. As for this appointment, on the 17th of June, this is a consequence of the fact that the existing rules on the classification of posts provided the -- that the deputy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said. The interpreters are unable to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Vlaski, you have to repeat that last part because the interpreters didn't catch it. You said: "As for this appointment, on the 17th of June, this is a consequence of the fact that the existing rules on the classification of posts ..." What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: According to the -- those rules, according to the classification of posts, the post of Deputy Chief of the Public Security Service is specified and, according to the agreement between the parties, should have been assigned to a member of the Serb ethnic group. After certain consultations - and I was unassigned, I was replaced from my previous post - I was proposed for this other post. And Minister Delimustafic signed that decision on appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, please, to August --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a moment, Your Honours. Forgive me, I'm just ... Yes, this is 65 ter 10269, please. I don't think this one is exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours, we have a objection to a number of these documents. I was waiting because we were not sure if the other -- the Prosecution actually intended to -- to exhibit these documents. Namely, there is six documents which have been disclosed on the 12th of February, on Friday, to us, for the very first time. And these documents, another three documents, including the one which Ms. Korner just called right now, are the exhibits -- or the -- the documents which are disclosed after the filing of the -- the pre-trial brief, so they are not on the 65 ter list. Now, I -- I know that the guide-line 15 requires the party to seek leave to use the material which has not -- which has not been timely noticed as the -- as the guide-line says. Now, apart from that, I believe the documents which have been disclosed just on last Friday for the very first time is -- is something which definitely, I think, that -- that the Office of the Prosecutor cannot show good cause for such -- such untimely disclosure of these documents. And -- and by this, Your Honours, we believe a certain prejudice to the accused is -- is created. I -- I can -- I can go on -- I have the arguments for this, but I don't -- I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to be as short as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have thought it would have been appropriate to raise this before the witness came into court and I began my examination. But having said that, all of the intercepts are in a database which are all on EDS. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But they would have to be notified about their use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They were -- yes, true. They were notified of their use in the disclosure. But, I mean, as I say, no objection was taken to this. And they were given copies, so they didn't have to look through the EDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a principal question. There -- we established -- or actually, Your Honours established the guide-lines. The guide-line number 6 says that this should be done by -- properly by a written motion in advance. Now, we -- we are now facing the situation as -- as -- as -- the Office of the Prosecutor is obviously understanding the situation as introducing the documents after the witness is -- after the witnesses pass. We have the motion which we are now responding to, pending one of the motions. So the -- the -- the documents are offered to -- for exhibits post festum, after the witnesses leave the courtroom, instead of doing it in advance. I think that's the only proper way how it should be done. And it has to be in a written motion because the guide-line says so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I can say is I appreciate what Your Honours said, and we're having them marked for identification. If absolutely required, we will apply to add them to the 65 ter list in a separate motion. But what is happening here is these are all documents about which the -- the witness can speak. And his name is mentioned. That's where they are all relevant. Whether they are entered into evidence as exhibits is another matter. All I'm asking is that he can deal with them. And not that -- we're not taking the Defence by surprise. One -- maybe one exception - I'm not sure there was an objection to this - there was an article in "Oslobodjenje," which we didn't find until last week sometime, although that's open source.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's six documents, including two videotapes, which have not been disclosed to us before Friday, never. I think that's -- speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels on both sides, we have had a look at the procedural guide-lines, and it appears that the Prosecution is required, first of all, to ensure that all documents that it intends to use are included in the 65 ter list; and, secondly, that documents which the Prosecution intends to use with the witness are notified to the Defence 72 hours in advance. And I think there is a rule also in the provision that says that prior to weekends it has to be on Thursday. So we do acknowledge that the Prosecution is out of time. However, you were notified on Friday that these six documents would be used, and you were given a copy. So I'm not sure that much prejudice has been caused, at least not in relation to this first document. What bothers the Bench is, rather, that at least this first document seems to have very little relevance. And this links up with the requirements that when the Prosecution has not sought introduction of a document on to its 65 ter list then it has to do so by doing two things. First of all, it has to show good cause and also it has to show that the document is relevant. And I'm not sure, at least I do not understand the immediate relevance of this transcript that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The intercept, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As -- Your Honours, it happens -- so happens that one doesn't matter because it's already an exhibit. This is it not the one that's being objected to. This is -- Your Honour, this is -- I'm going to show the -- the -- through the series of intercepts, what happened to Mr. Vlaski. This is the first that shows him being appointed. It also -- you know -- I mean, I'm not going to make a speech about why it's relevant. But, in fact, it's already -- this one's an exhibit. It's the next one that was about to come up that Mr. Zecevic is objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add, Your Honours. And I completely agree with the analysis that the Chamber has -- has just stated, that I just -- we are really concerned with -- with the -- with -- with this, because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I must add that this is the one issue that has taken up most of our time when discussing procedural matters. And I -- it's beginning to become a nuisance to the Court that we have to go through this far too often. And I must remind the Prosecution of its obligation to ensure that documents are provided according to the procedural guide-lines that we have set up. I'm sorry. We cannot go on like this, because we lose so much time. So that's the general instruction that the Chamber wishes to hand down at the moment; namely, please observe what we have set in place in terms of use of documents and notification of the Defence. Now, in the concrete matter of the six documents, the Chamber is unable to assess the good cause that the Prosecution may have, and we are also unable to assess the relevance of the documents. And so, for these reasons, we are unable to determine whether any prejudice has been made to the Defence. We are prepared to allow the Prosecution to use these documents with the witness, provided that we come to the conclusion that the Defence does not suffer any prejudice. But we have to see the documents before we can make any final determination of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that mean Your Honours want to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all those documents, the list and the documents, are all with Your Honours. Do Your Honours want to look at them before we carry on? Because I'm going through the whole -- I'm getting it through now, I say in terms, I think it's about five or six, if not more, intercepts to show what happened. Some of which are on our 65 ter list, others which are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the Legal Officer reminds me that the document that is currently on the screen, namely, the intercept in which Dr. Karadzic is speaking to Mr. Mandic, has not been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, my information, Your Honour, I don't know who's right, but my information is it is exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if I may, before the witness is ushered in. There are two things, Your Honours. Regarding the request by the Trial Chamber to state our position in relation to Witnesses ST-179 and ST-123, we do not object for subpoena of these two witnesses. And one additional thing: I was notified by my assistants that 1D176 document which was MFI'd pending translation, I was informed that the translation was received and now I move that -- and it is updated in e-court, that particular number, and I move the Court to lift the MFI now and properly exhibit it as 1D176. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, Zupljanin Defence take no position with regard to the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber has deliberated on the objection raised by the Defence before the break, and we have reached the following conclusion, and I will explain afterwards why we have come to this conclusion. The documents presented Friday afternoon by the Prosecution included a list of documents to be used with the current witness. In this list, nine documents appeared to have been proposed for use, although these nine documents had not been previously included in the 65 ter list. The general rule that the Chamber has laid down in the procedural guide-lines is that no documents can be used or can be introduced into evidence unless it has been included in the 65 ter list; or, if it has not, then, unless the moving party has shown good cause for the delay and also has shown that the document is relevant. In the present case, the Chamber has not been given any explanation as to why the nine documents have not previously been included in the 65 ter list, nor have we been given any indication of their relevance. And the determination of the Chamber is, therefore, that a distinction could be made between those documents among the nine new documents that have already been released to the public domain, and those of the nine documents that have previously been MFI'd by virtue of their being introduced through other witnesses can be used today with this witness, whereas, the remaining three documents cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... which three? Sorry, Your Honour, which three documents are those? Which those three documents are those, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Document 25, 26, and 28 have been already released into the public domain. They are articles and TV clips. And then as for the intercepts, we've been told that three of them have already been MFI'd. So that's three intercepts and three public domain documents, altogether six documents that can be used today with this witness, and the remaining three documents out of the nine cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I'm just asking which of the three that can't, rather, than telling me which I can. Because at the moment I can't work out which ones Your Honours are referring to. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We do not, at the moment, have a final updated list of which of the intercepts that have been MFI'd. This is why I'm speaking in -- in -- in some misty terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, Your Honour, none of the ones -- can I tell Your Honours which the intercepts are. The first is 10266, 10267, 10269, which you can forget about because I can see that it is going take some time. 10270, they're all ones that have not been MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is clear. But three of them have been MFI'd as far as we are told. So one of them is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, in that case, that surprises me, because when we checked, we didn't think they had been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yeah. Couldn't Mr. Smith ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right -- we don't think -- no, no the Case Manager did a check. I heard Your Honours' remark. And we don't think any of the ones that are in -- if you have looked at the list on the screen, you'll see they're written in red, yes. I don't see them in black and white. But none of those have been MFI'd. Can I -- I don't think I -- I don't want to waste time while the witness is sitting here again. But can I explain. They're part of a series of intercepts, all of which deal with Mr. Vlaski's position, all of which he has listened to. And some went on to our list but others didn't, and it was only when we were checking the intercept lists that we realised they weren't in there. But it shows a -- the progression, if you like, from the 16th of September to the 19th, and it's relevant to Mr. Karadzic's reaction. You have looked at some of those. This shows the progression through. And that's -- that's the only reason we're putting it in, because it's clearly quite important. It starts with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Zepinic, moves through Mrs. Plavsic and whatever, and that's why we think it's important. But if Your Honours say I can't, then I'm not going argue at all. But none of those have been MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So they cannot be used?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I just -- the reason being, because of the late disclosure or the late notification. Or just -- you can't use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You can't use them because you did not move to have them admitted into your 65 ter list. And this was particularly detrimental to the Defence because in all the other cases which we have dealt with, we have been dealing with 92 ter witnesses; whereas, today we're dealing with a viva voce witness. Now in the 92 ter instances, the Defence has been given a 92 ter package way in advance which would have enabled the Defence to prepare itself for the cross-examination of those 92 ter witnesses. But, today, this is a viva voce witness, and the Defence is being taken by surprise by virtue of your late disclosure and by virtue of the fact that you didn't apply or didn't move to have them included in your 65 ter list. And then comes on top of it the issue of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that's -- as it were, the objection wasn't taken. Either we weren't notified in advance, and they've had this since Friday. And you didn't ask me to explain the relevance. And I can explain the relevance by showing them to you. If you don't look at them, whether or not they're admitted as exhibits and whether Mr. Vlaski [sic], you cannot see the progression of what happened. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the Chamber, of course, is not suggesting or intending to imply that the -- in this case, Office of the Prosecutor, is deliberately trying to sabotage the way that the guide-lines were intended to move the trial along. It's only that at the end of the day we come to -- we come down the side the fact that the guide-lines are there and there are consequences. As Judge Harhoff says, the lack of notice, the lack of effective notice, to the Defence and the -- and the Chamber has -- has this -- has these consequences. So, therefore, that is why the distinction was made in the ruling that has been -- that has been given, between the public domain documents where the same technical objection could have been taken, but, effectively, the Chamber has waved that, and the documents which have been otherwise MFI'd when we draw the line between those and the others. And I think we should -- we have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour -- all right. I apologise. But, I simply cannot see why, because the video cassette is in public, the video is of a news reel or was in a newspaper, we gave exactly the same notice to the Defence that we were intending to use them that -- that the distinction is drawn like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the distinction drawn in your favour. We could have ruled out all those documents because of no -- no motion has been filed to have them on the 65 ter list. So simply -- so simply as that. We said we still can take those two -- three or four in, because, well, the damage is -- is less for the Defence because they are in the public domain, because they already have been discussed, and MFI'd. But that's only -- only for -- for this time, you know. Next time, documents will go out if they are not on the 65 ter list or if there is not a prior -- a motion to have them on the 65 ter list prior to -- for the use in court and tendering the documents, even for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all right. I -- Mr. Vlaski is in here. But, Your Honours, there simply has not been a single policy being followed throughout this case. And filing of motions in and I respectively say in our judgement, just merely adds to the ever growing pile -- I mean, if that's what Your Honours' ruling is, I'm not -- not seeking to, at this stage, take it any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vlaski, I'm sorry about all this. I'm afraid we're going to have to start moving fairly quickly through your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We should have up on the screen now, please, an intercept which is on, which is already an exhibit, P902.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, this is a intercept I think you listened to. And were you able to identify, recognise, both the voices of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Zepinic? I'm afraid you have to say yes or no. Oh, you're not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: [In English] Translate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. On the screen, you can see the transcript of one of the tapes you've listened to. You were able to recognise, I believe, both the voices of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Zepinic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look, please, at the second page in English and the third -- second page in B/C/S. Sorry, the third page in B/C/S, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karadzic is talking --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this is completely different. Your Honours, I'm sorry. Can we go back -- I'm so sorry. Can we go back, please, to the first page in English. Can we go back to the first page in English, please. Yup, it's different. I'm sorry, Your Honour. What I have been -- what I have got in my binder is different, but this is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, Mr. Zepinic is telling Mr. Karadzic that he got drunk with you that night and he goes -- Mr. Zepinic says to Mr. Karadzic that he found out about the decision on the replacement of Nedjo Vlaski on Friday. Now, this is the 16th of September. Can you tell us, please, what had happened to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Apparently, my case was interesting at the time, as it is now. And let me clarify what this was all about. Because of the position to which I was supposed to be appointed to, in view of that position, you can clearly see the situation in MUP and the personnel policy run within it. It also -- it is also indicative of the relations between the various political parties and between the various appointed officials in the ministry. Let me clarify. I received, from Mr. Delimustafic, a decision to the post of the Deputy Chief of the State Security Service. However, I was unable to take over the duties that I was supposed to take over, pursuant to this decision, because the head of that same security service, Mr. Kvesic, the one that I was supposed to be a deputy to, placed obstacles in the way of this. This must have been deliberate, because otherwise such an act of arbitrariness and self-will is difficult to explain. This was the dimension to my case because within the hierarchy under the rules the entire operative work of the security sector of the State Security Service in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be controlled from this particular post that I was supposed to take over. And that is why somebody objected to the fact that the Serbs should have someone occupying this post. Therefore, I was obstructed in an attempt to take up the new position. Alongside this, there was legal obstruction taking place, the aim of which was to eliminate this post from the official classification of jobs. Those who were behind this attempt made a new version of the rules overnight and sent it to the government of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina for their approval. In other words, the rules were changed on my account, so that the post to which I was appointed was simply deleted with -- physically with a white varnish, and they tasked the minister with providing a written explanation that would account for such deletion. The minister signed an explanation, which stated that the process of rationalising leadership posts was taking place. However, it was only my post that was abolished in the new version of the rules. By the logic of things, the lower post should have been abolished as well. What was important to them was to -- to discontinue the chain within the hierarchy of posts occupied by Serbs. The initiative thus formulated was easily carried by the government, because it was the HDZ/SDA coalition which had the majority votes in the government. So the government basically abolished the post of the Deputy Chief of the security sector. Consequently, the division appointing me to this post was null and void. In this way, the Serbs lost yet another position, in addition to the position that I had held earlier on. Therefore, we could not wield any sort of influence on the work of the service, save for several insignificant posts that we still held. In this way, we were humiliated, demoted in an unlawful way. But there was no way to reverse the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So, this is what Mr. Zepinic is telling Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, in this intercept to the third page in B/C/S, and I'm -- I need to see the English. Try the third page, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there that Karadzic is getting quite cross about it, and we've had a look at this intercept before. And then he says: "Please let Vlaski get in touch with me and tell him not to leave." Now, did you get in touch with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I did not, because I realised it would have been pointless. The position of Mr. Karadzic, who did not get into state institutions, he was the only one who remained only a political figure as a president of the political party, unlike Izetbegovic and others, who got positions in the government. His position at the time was a marginal one. He had no power, unlike others who had absolute power on the government. And you can see what sort of power he has, or absence thereof, here because he says to the deputy police minister who, in his turn, again, didn't have that much power because he was answerable to the police minister, to use his offices to do this and that. Again, he was appealing to the deputy minister who depended on the kindness and mercy of the minister for favours but was otherwise under no obligation to do what he was asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Vlaski, I'm really sorry, but it was a simple question: Did you get in touch with Dr. Karadzic as he tells Dr. Zepinic you should do?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I said right away that I didn't, because he didn't have any influence to excerpt. And I didn't think that I -- that anything would come out of it, save for me meeting up with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the influence that he may or may not have had, according to you. Then he ends up by saying, Mr. Karadzic, on that page: "Please find Vlaski and let him write a complaint on the decision. He should hand it to you personally, and you should act according to it." Did you write a complaint about the decision?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That would have been absurd to address any sort of letter to individuals who are disrespectful of the law and to expect them to take my letter or complaint into consideration in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you neither wrote to Mr. Delimustafic nor to Dr. Zepinic nor to anybody else. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Of course I didn't. It wasn't my personal problem; it was the problem of the institution run by individuals who were either incompetent to do the job or were under the influence of others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When you were listening to intercepts yesterday, did you listen to one where Biljana Plavsic was also talking to Dr. Karadzic about you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I heard the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you also know Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: For the same reasons that I knew all the other officials in the government, I was under the obligation to take care of their security. So I knew and had occasion to meet Madam Plavsic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And once you were in Belgrade dealing with the Vila Bosanka later on in 1992, did you see a great deal of Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: No. As she came out of Sarajevo in the month of May and she was the last one to leave her flat in the area of Jahorina, it was only later on that she went to Belgrade because she had certain obligations to attend to in the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in Belgrade and you were in Belgrade, did you see her on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Not on a regular basis, but I did have the opportunity to see her from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right did. You recognise her voice when you heard it on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, indeed, did she tell you -- did she tell Mr. Karadzic that the complaint was that you had been replaced by a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: She complained, and that is just an indication of the powerlessness of the top bearers of state authority of the representatives of the Serbian people, because Biljana Plavsic was the president of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, a person who was a figure at the head of a state body which was in charge of monitoring and directing the work of state security. In that body and in the Presidency, because of the manner of decision-making, she had no influence in those functions and could not have an influence on anything. So her protest and her dissatisfaction about my case and many other matters and acts and relationship towards her as an organ of authority shown in the Presidency and in the party which had placed her in this position. This was just a reflection of the powerlessness of officials to carry out their duties pursuant to the law because of conduct, obstructionism, which were impossible to react to in any other way, other than just plain dissatisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So it's your view that none of the Serb people in authority, even in the Presidency, had any power or influence at all. Is that -- is that what you're saying and have been saying throughout this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Absolutely, that was the main reason why everything had been placed into question, because a constitutional people and their legally elected representatives did not have the opportunity to carry out the most basic duties, pursuant to the regulations, the constitution, and the laws. If anyone needed to privatise Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- and exclude arbitrarily one people, then that would have been the way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, I think you also listened, and this is all the same day, to a conversation between Karadzic and Koljevic, all the 17th of September. And, again, was Karadzic speaking to Koljevic, on the intercept you listened to, about your case?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. It was also a question of my case because Koljevic was one of the members of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, representing the Serb people, and he, just like professor Plavsic, were academically educated, cultivated people and were not used to the method of work that was prevalent in the Presidency and probably were not used to the attitude towards them by representatives who had arrived there according to God knows what criteria and positions previously held. So my problem was just mentioned as something to be noted in order to have one more reason why they would need to request a political response to such a situation or to seek a political response to such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up intercept, same day, all these intercepts, 17th of September, P903, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a conversation - we can all see 17th September - between Mr. Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Simovic. Can [sic] you listen to that? Were you able to recognise both voices?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Simovic both. I know Mr. Simovic too, because we worked together on the same duties in the security service in Sarajevo, so I did recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to you look, please, at what Mr. Karadzic says in the middle of the page where he is speaking to Mr. Simovic. "Would you please tell Zepinic that tomorrow we are withdrawing all of our ministers and all of our officials in the MUP. We are discontinuing the complete partnership and going into opposition because Zepinic is allowing maltreatment and removal from office of our men. Vlaski was removed from his office and it is over. Tonight at 8.00, I am going to break up with Izetbegovic. I am withdrawing everything. SDS party into opposition." And so on and so forth. You said that Mr. Karadzic had no power to effect what happened to you. As far as you were concerned, did he have the power to withdraw the SDS, though, from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: You can see that this is an emotional reaction by a man who doesn't have a response to these nasty things that were done not only to me but towards political colleagues and to my people to whom I belong by birth. So I experienced this fate. And Mr. Karadzic's reaction is just a consequence of an emotional state and the fact that an end must be put to such a position. So what would be the point of him being at the head of the party, which placed him in power, if he could not implement this power in any way? You do not respond to power with a telephone call. He couldn't tell Mr. Zepinic in a telephone call that he was going to do this and that. There has to be some sort of an assessment before embarking on such an activity. So I would say that this was an emotional reaction by a figure that was in -- in power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... right. It may be emotional. All I asked you, Mr. Vlaski, was whether Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic had the power to walk out of the Assembly, taking the SDS with him.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: At the time, the conditions were not there nor was the point of tolerance so low for such an act to ensue. This act ensued later, and this was done because there was no other way out, other than what was discussed, and for which he had the support of the other representatives of the Serbian people in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then as things appeared, then in the other institutions of power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all those representatives who participated in power. They all sought the protection of the party which had one -- its share of the votes in the election, in order to be able to implement their share of power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just look, please, at the bottom of the page in -- no, second page in English and second page, also, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what he's going on to say at the top: "Vlaski was the straw that broke the camel's back. I'm going to phone Hebib to tell him this, and you tell Zepinic that it is over." And then to resign. Did you listen, in fact, also to an intercept where Karadzic did ring Mr. Hebib about what was happening to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, the following day -- no, the same day, I'm sorry, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe it was ruled by the Trial Chamber. I don't think that Ms. Korner is going to use this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh okay. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not using the documents that I have been ruled that I can't use. I'm dealing with the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document has been ruled out, and she wants -- Ms. Korner wants to use the contents of the document so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told me I can't put the documents in as exhibits or indeed even introduce them. Can I -- with the greatest of respect, I can certainly ask this witness what he heard and listened to this morning or yesterday. If Your Honours are ruling that I can't even ask him that, then that's a different matter entirely. Then I will seek to argue this much more fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we think we appreciate your -- I shouldn't use the word difficulty, but I can't think of any other word, and we fully understand the objection that is taken by the Defence, in that the course that you are following strongly suggests that, notwithstanding the ruling that the Chamber has given in terms of the admissibility of these documents, that you are nevertheless going to effectively get the contents in. However, we do appreciate the relevance of your seeking to elicit from the witness what he did and why he did it. So we would rule that if you concentrate on what he did and why he did it, then that would -- even if that brings you very close to that line, that you may proceed down that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That we will be filing an application to add these documents to our 65 ter list. By that stage, the witness will have gone. He can also recognise - and I underline that again - and it may well we can get these intercepts even without adding to the 65 ter list the other evidence we are going to call. But I won't be able to get that evidence in. All -- however, I take the point. Your Honours, what I'm prepared to do is say he listened to intercepts, was able to recognise the voices, and what he did as a result of it. Well, I see Your Honour Judge Delvoie shaking his head. But, Your Honour, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I refer now to what the witness did back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking to what -- he listened to all the intercepts yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, but isn't the ruling that the intercepts are out?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The ruling is the intercepts are out until such time as I call evidence about their quality. But I was told the ruling was I could ask about recognition of voices. That was absolutely clear. Your Honours, we can go back and find it. That was Your Honours' ruling. I specifically asked that -- Your Honours, regardless of whether I get the intercepts admitted -- I know Mr. Zecevic is waiting to say something, but regardless -- we're now being completely side tracked. Regardless of whether the intercepts are admitted at this stage as exhibits if the party to it is not the one giving evidence, I was specifically told I could ask someone who was aware of the contents and who had knowledge of the speakers whether they recognised the voices. And that -- I know Your Honours don't seem to feel at the moment that's important. My respectful suggestion is it may well turn out to be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are we talking now about previously MFI'd intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We're talking about the intercepts which you have ruled I cannot have in at the moment but which he has listened to and which we're going to apply to put in. But he won't be here to give the evidence that he is able to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. It's -- again, we're coming back to the position -- the founding position when I -- when I first made the objection. It's all about the notice. We are not on notice about these documents. That's why the Trial Chamber ruled. Now Ms. Korner is - I'm sorry to say this - but trying to open a side door to, I don't know, introduce these documents again. I don't think -- I'm sorry, but I don't think that's -- that's proper. The ruling has been given, and we should at least honour that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think Judge Delvoie put it very clearly: The ruling is that these documents cannot be used today with this witness, including your being prevented from showing it to him. Now, I must say that, just as one of the three Judges on the Bench, I'm -- I'm not quite certain that I understand just why and how this is important and relevant, as you claim it is.
