So my suggestion is that you address the issue of the various attempts made by each of the three political groupings in Sarajevo at the time to seize control over the administration directly with the witness, and you will have to do that without using these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour, we really are -- and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am slightly concerned, and I -- but I don't think it's proper for me to make a speech at this stage, and particularly in front of the witness, about why this is relevant. And it's nothing to -- or very little to do with what is described as the resting control over the SUP in Sarajevo. This is, I appreciate, the witness is saying, but it's -- it's not that exactly. I don't think it's right to make speeches at this stage about why we say it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Certainly it is for the witnesses to testify and not the counsels. But I think what you have just said explains the problem very well, because if this is not all about the power struggle in those days in 1992 over the control over the state administration, then I don't -- really don't know what it is about then. So ... There is a major --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is a major problem of understanding where we are going.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm perfectly - I think the witness ought to leave - but I'm perfectly prepared to explain that. I mean, I don't, as I say, I don't think it's proper for the Prosecution to make speeches in the middle of trial any more than we have objected to the Defence making speeches. But if it's not clear to Your Honours, then I think I ought to -- then I ought to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Couldn't you put the questions to the witness that will exemplify and bring out the evidence that you wish?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can certainly put questions to him. Yes, but... right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the speech you -- you're not willing to make is, if I understand it well, about relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But I think that what happens due to the fact that we consider that the 65 ter list rule is not applied correctly is not about relevance. So the speech about relevance, even if you made it, would not be relevant, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think we're somewhat -- we're now -- I'm so sorry, Your Honour, but I think we're at cross purposes. But, in any event, I think the best thing is I proceed as -- as His Honour Judge Harhoff has said with questions to the witness leaving out any reference to the intercepts which you have ruled out. But can I make it absolutely clear, Your Honours, there will be an application to put it on the 65 ter list. There will be an application that these are authentic, genuine intercepts. And this witness is in the best position, because of his knowledge of the participates and what they're talking about, to authentic those intercepts. And that's -- I just want to make that absolutely clear. Right. Can we move on, please, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one comment, Your Honours. Your Honours, the guide-line says that the application has to be made in advance, in written form. So if the Prosecution thinks this witness will be able to give them this data which is important for their case, they should have filed the application as according to the guide-lines. I don't think that it would be proper that we -- that the witness leaves and then only afterwards, post-facto, the Prosecution files the application. I don't think that's proper. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I may respond. You are absolutely right, Mr. Zecevic. But that is a matter of admission into evidence. At the moment, we're dealing with this witness, who has to provide us with evidence about the events that took place at the relevant time in 1992. So let's get on with that, and then we can always return to the issue of whether or not these and other intercepts can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And notwithstanding the extended break that we had earlier, it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we rise, on the 22nd of January, 2010, the Trial Chamber issued an order for safe conduct for Witness ST-186, stating that as the witness is scheduled to travel between 6 and 12 February 2010, any change of date will be communicated to the witness and the state authorities by the Registrar of the Tribunal, and any notice of such change shall form part of and have the same binding force and effect as this order for safe conduct. During hearing of the 3rd of February, 2010, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that, following amendments in this schedule, ST-187 is required to be in The Hague between the 6th and the 13th of March, 2010, instead. The Trial Chamber requests the Registry to make the necessary arrangements to implement the order for safe conduct for ST-187 accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, were you aware, at the time, that the Serb leadership, Bosnian Serb leadership, or the SDS leadership, was taking such an interest in your fate?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: On listening to the intercepts, I concluded that perhaps they were attributed to much of a historic importance, and I'm referring to the situation I was in. The fact of the matter is that the problems did escalate and warrant a reaction on the part of the political structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You heard the learned Judge describe this as a struggle for the control of the MUP. What was the importance of who was controlling the MUP in Bosnia at this stage, in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The struggle for the control of the MUP was won right at the start by the party which had been given the possibility by the election results to be allocated posts in the MUP. The significance of the MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of how one might view it as a state, was enormous because the MUP was the only armed force at the time. The political parties, which were contemplating the creation of the state and government, were capable of gauging its significance. Evidently the SDS did not have that ability to gauge its importance when it was getting into this discussion with its other coalition partners as to the allocation of posts. The consequence of such an approach on the part of the SDS is illustrated by my case and by other cases where some other forces were in control and at play which used unlawful means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But you say at the time, when the allocation of posts was going on, the SDS didn't appreciate the importance the MUP, in your view. At this stage, however, when you have heard and seen that from Karadzic through to the members of the Presidency there was a lot of discussion and threats going on. By that stage, were the SDS leadership aware of the importance of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It did become aware, but that -- it was far too late. It was water under the bridge. They wanted to change matters at the eleventh hour, at the time when they were already losing three to nil. They did not take control of vital post in the institutions. They did not take measures to make sure, at least, that -- or, rather, to make sure that unlawful actions did not take place. The upshot was that one individual who was at the head of the institution, such as state security, the chief of the State Security Service, embodied all the three branches of powers, because once -- one, for instance, the individual at the head of the Bihac state security was an MP, he was a member of the parliament, and, at the same time, he was the chief of the service which was part of the executive branch. By virtue of his position as an MP, he should have been the one to control the legality of the work of the service which he headed. So they were individuals holding posts that were of very great importance, and they held all these various posts in the different branches of government which allowed them to carry their activities wilfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It was a simple question and doesn't require that length of answer. Your view is that the SDS realised too late the important of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal -- let's go back to what you were doing then, please. I think it's right that, in early 1992, were you assigned to the administration for intelligence and counter-intelligence in -- in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: This occurred after the ploy where my post of the deputy head was abolished. Another similar situation occurred to me shortly thereafter when I was replaced from the position of the chief of the administration for the security of persons and facilities; that was once. And then again from the position of the chief of service. At that point, I didn't have a position to hold, and so they assigned me to the post of an inspector to the administration you mentioned, the administration for intelligence and counter-intelligence. And I held the post of an inspector there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of your activities there, did you take trips to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade previously as well. I don't recall the specific dates. I didn't go there very often. But for various, both personal and professional reasons, I -- I would go there. So I would go there because I had relatives there and also because of the situation concerning the Serb representation in the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I had to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When you went there, did you go from time to time with Dragan Devedlaka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. We went there together on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have meetings there with the predecessor to Jovica Stanisic as head of state security, a gentleman named Zoran Janackovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Before coming across Mr. Zoran Janackovic, we had Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic as our contact. He was the minister of the MUP in Serbia. As for Mr. Janackovic, we had a meeting with him later; the goal being to simply brief one another on the situations in the respective countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said "... because of the situation concerning the Serb" -- I don't think you said "reputation" -- because of the "situation." Because of the situation concerning the Serb situation in the government. What was the concern?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: There was several reasons, or concerns. Firstly, the staffing policy, which was detrimental to the Serb people, and various manipulations and ploys on the part of the colleagues who enjoyed the political sponsorship and support of the parties of the SDA and HDZ, as well as the general state of security in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina had, by that time, been getting into an ever deeper crisis. Those of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I mean the Serb personnel, felt helpless. The Serb policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina lost any power it may have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Serbia was preoccupied with its own problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you ask them for any assistance in terms of arms or equipment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: This wasn't our job, and we didn't have any discussions on this issue. The Serbs were engaged in the Yugoslav People's Army, which were, in the view of others, pro-Serbian because most of its members were Serbs, and they didn't need weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I move now, please, to the meeting of the 11th of February in Banja Luka which you attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the number of which is ... yes. It's -- for some reason it's Defence Exhibit 1D135. Now, you had a chance to read it both when you were interviewed in Banja Luka and again two days ago. But I think, as you told us in Banja Luka, you remember this meeting as though it were yesterday. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Well, I do remember it. Unfortunately, we hadn't had such meetings until February of 1992. Had we had an opportunity to meet up earlier on, matters would have been better. We met for the first time at that point, and there were several among those who were in attendance who I didn't know from before. I think more than half of them were unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This was a meeting, was it, that was open only to Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Well, no. There were some individuals who weren't Serbs. They came from mixed marriages. Though, let's put it that way, they were loyal to the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Which ones came from mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nenad Radovic, and I'm not sure about Igor Velasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who asked to you come to the meeting, or how did you find out about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: As for the circle of individuals whom I was more often in touch with, they were mostly colleagues from state security who held positions in the structure: Dragan Devedlaka, Mr. Goran Radovic, then Goran Zugic. Yes, Dragan Devedlaka, I mentioned him already. So this was the circle of people working for state security, and that's why we were more often in touch. And I learned about this meeting from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they tell you, either Radovic or Devedlaka, who had asked them to attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I don't remember. The atmosphere at that point was that the people who attended the meeting were brought together by common problems all of us were faced with. This was an attempt to do something, and that was one of the goals of this meeting. We found that out only when we arrived in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Why was the meeting held in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I don't think there was a particular reason behind it. At least that was my impression. And I didn't organise the meeting. In my view, the meeting could have held [as interpreted] anywhere, at any of the locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When you look at the composition of the people who gathered there and if you consider the security aspect, I think this could have been the case. But probably because of the logistics and accommodation facilities and some other reasons perhaps, it was suggested that it be held in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may well have been. But given that Sarajevo was where the seat of government was, why not in Sarajevo as opposed to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The location is not of decisive importance for a meeting to be held. Banja Luka was characterised by a more normal, as it were, situation, when it came to the MUP institution. And I'm referring to the Banja Luka Security Centre which proved much simpler because the MUP staff in Banja Luka were much more loyal. And I'm referring to Mr. Zupljanin, who was the head of the centre. This must have decided the matter. It was a centre which covered a vast area and was characterised by a more positive, favourable political and security situation. Otherwise, it could have been held in Sarajevo, Pale, Sokolac, anywhere, it could not have been relevant for any other aspects than the atmosphere that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Loyal to whom? "... the ... staff in Banja Luka were much more loyal. And I'm referring to Mr. Zupljanin ..." Loyal to whom?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The law and its implementation. If you have a leader, a leader at the -- one of the top positions, such a leader should have the highest responsibility. If you have an individual who is not responsible higher up than those who are lower up [as interpreted] are left to their own devices and can conduct themselves as they wish. We had instances of unlawfulness in Sarajevo, in the very head office and all the way down to field officers, various commanders of stations, et cetera. And, of course, this wasn't something that allowed for loyalty. It was the professionals themselves who directed the way in which all the subordinates would comport themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tell me something, Mr. Vlaski, what was the ethnic composition in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, a part of the answer of the witness didn't -- wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the last part. He was -- he was referring to the chain of command, something. I don't want to actually influence the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you ask the witness to repeat his -- the last part of his answer to your last question, please. Last but one questions -- well, your last question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, can you repeat your answer. Not -- please don't repeat your answer. The last -- the last sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I think that the problem lay in the relationship along the chain of command in the police which should follow subordination; where the chain of command did not function in a lawful way, anarchy ensued. In other words, everyone did what they felt was due and interpreted the law in their own way and would not incur any responsibility or consequences because they enjoy political protection at the post that they held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back to the question that I asked next. What was the ethnic composition in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the last sentence, he said, It wasn't case in Banja Luka is not recorded, so I must suggest ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. What wasn't?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, can we leave this whole topic. Can we get to this. Is -- what was the ethnic composition, please, Mr. Vlaski, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I don't have and cannot recall the demographic data for Banja Luka. I can tell you what the level -- what the situation at the level of Banja Luka was when it came to the division of power. As for Banja Luka itself, I am not in a position to give you a specific answer, a precise answer. Are we referring to Banja Luka proper, the Banja Luka region, the Krajina? Demographics differ, and I don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The previous answer -- the last sentence that the witness said when he was talking about the way in which the various MUP structures behaved, he said that that was not -- that did not apply to Banja Luka, the unlawfulness of conduct. And that's important. So I would like the witness to kindly repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat your -- I'm not sure which answer this question was to. Mr. Krgovic, where are we in terms of line numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... sorry, page 59, line 6. This part is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that is so far back that you are probably going to have ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask the question again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that in my cross-examination, so that's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I ask you to refresh your memory from your interview, Mr. Vlaski, in Banja Luka generally, did any one of the nations in -- in Bosnia have a majority?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: As for Banja Luka proper, the Serbs were at a numerical advantage. Let's put it that way. But I don't have the statistics that would indicate the various settlements encompassed by Banja Luka and their ethnic makeup. It is a rather thankless task now to manipulate the various numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the fact that Banja Luka had a Serb majority and a Serb chief of the CSB have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I can finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the fact that Banja Luka had a Serb majority and a Serb chief of the CSB have anything to do with that being the place for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It could have had an impact on that. I'm not stating it did. It just could have, for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mico Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner. I understand this meeting was a meeting in the RS MUP; is that correct, Mr. Witness? It was an RS MUP meeting on the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the minutes, it follows that the meeting was held in Banja Luka on such and such a date, and those who attended the meeting are listed here. According to the minutes, the meeting did not have an institutional format. I could say it was a meeting of a group, a working meeting of a group of individuals of Serb ethnicity. And this is something that you will see from the discussion as it unfolded and the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I will give the floor back to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so we are absolutely clear, everybody who attended that meeting was a Serb member of the MUP and a relatively high-up Serb member of the MP. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: One could interpret it in this way between the lines. But for none of those attendees do we have a title, and nowhere in the discussion was the issue raised of the institutions that they were representing there and who they were speaking -- on whose behalf they were speaking. As I can tell from the minutes, they all spoke on their own personal behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting this was an officially called meeting at all, Mr. Vlaski. This was a meeting, as we can see from the minutes, where discussion was held by these individuals but all of whom held relatively high positions. For example, Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, --

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Zupljanin opened the meeting, as we can see. Do you know why he spoke first? Was it simply because the meeting was in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It is only logical and natural that an individual hosting an event for a number of persons should open the meeting, should give some opening remarks. And I think it's the sole reason why he did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the meeting -- where was the meeting actually held in Banja Luka? In the CSB?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: You don't have to suggest places to me. It was not held on the premises that were intended for the work of the police or the MUP. It was held on the first floor of the Bosna Hotel, right next to the piano bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic spoke second. Do you know why he took apparently a fairly leading role in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It was logical for someone who came from Sarajevo and represented or held a significant position within the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina who, in addition to that, had greater responsibility for representing interests to do that. He was, perhaps, in a better position than everyone else to take up that role at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've read through the minutes. Are those accurate minutes of the meeting that were taken by Mr. Velasevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I think the discussion went beyond that which is recorded here, although the minutes reflect the state of affairs. There may have been certain formulations that -- well, had audio recording been made of the meeting, then, perhaps, the -- it would be a full reflection of it. But I don't think that the minutes are far from that, far from reflecting reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So they're, obviously, as you say, a summary of what was said. But as far as that summary goes, an accurate one. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Among other things that were said, Mr. Koroman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the third page in English, please, and the third page in B/C/S -- fourth page in B/C/S, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- said that his opinion was that: "All further discussion is pointless. A list of demands should be made drawn up," as opposed to drown up, "and given to the MUP with a deadline. If they are not met, we must paralyse the whole of SRBH and we can do that." Can you just tell the Judges who Mr. Koroman was?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Malko Koroman was the official at the head of a police organisational unit in Pale, public security unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Tutus spoke, and then you spoke: "We must work out how to carry out the decisions from this meeting the only way would be to organise the Serbian MUP and implement all decisions without question."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of the -- of the witness, it's on the next page. His speech is on the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Thank you. Yes, can we go to the next page then. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was your view, in February of 1992, as you expressed it, that there was really only one thing to do, and that was to organise a separate MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: If I can respond to this question, these discussions and conclusions show that Serbian representatives offered the possibility of making one more effort and to change the situation and the relations in the MUP, because the conclusions from this meeting were supposed to be and were sent to Minister Delimustafic and the Muslim, Bosniak, Croatian representatives who had usurped this institution. What we were left with was to offer them a chance of an agreement; are we going to embark together on setting up a lawful institution, or are we going to go, as the political process was already unfolding, to the development of our own institutions, which was supposed to protect the people we represented, because this could not be done from the institution that already existed. That is why is this meeting occur in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's turn to conclusions, please, which is on the last page of the -- no, sorry. The penultimate page in English. Fourth page and ... it's the following page in B/C/S than this one we're on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where in the conclusions we're able to find the Serbian representatives offering the possibility of making one more effort.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The first conclusion: "A Serbian collegium is hereby established in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Not a MUP but Serbian collegium consisting of Serbian personnel at executive positions along all the lines of work within the MUP. Precisely the reason why we were bypassed and humiliated because our representatives did not occupy a single significant function. We were skipped over, ignored. So what else could we do but make a composition that would be able to meet regularly, be part of the MUP entity, and be able to protect the legitimacy and legality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Second conclusion: The Serbian MUP [as interpreted], or Deputy Minister Momcilo Mandic would manage the Serbian collegium and ensure the implementation of decisions. Because, at that time, he was the only representative in that institution representing the Serbian people. And then the third conclusion: "The Serbian collegium," again, the collegium is underscored. It's an informal circle, gathered every morning, or twice a week, depending on the situation, and that was the practice in the police where it would then review all the questions, and it says that that Serbian collegium would "carry out all the necessary preparations for the functioning of the Serbian MUP after the promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So that is the third conclusion. So it's an alternative. The first or the second -- and if the first and second conclusions were not implemented, then there is nothing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Pantelic wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for everyone in these proceedings. It's just a correction to the transcript. It's page 65, line 12, after the word "second conclusion," witness said the Serbian "member." It's not correct. Said in the LiveNote the Serbian MUP. The right expression was Serbian member. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, I can't even -- I can't make sense of anything that's been written there. It says the Serbian collegium would carry out all the necessary preparation for the -- I imagine all that gobbldygook must be "functioning of the Serbian MUP."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vlaski, this is the whole point, isn't it? If you look at paragraph 3, this wasn't anything, was it? I mean, sorry, to do with, as you put it, the last chance. One and two were set up in order to carry out the preparations necessary for the functioning of the Serbian MUP after the promulgation of the Serbian republic. Can you explain why you say that is an olive branch, if you like, to the BiH MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: May I reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Conclusion number 5 states: "Not a single decision regarding the staffing policies in the SRBH MUP," I underline the SRBH MUP, "will be implemented without the approval of Deputy Minister Momcilo Mandic." This conclusion contradicts these other conclusions, but it's a conclusion. So that means that there still was a possibility to make appointments pursuant to these principles that should have been in effect for an institution of this nature. And that in itself would have placed out of commission these conclusions that were forced by such an attitude towards the Serbian people, generally in Bosnia and Herzegovina and towards us as professionals, and those heading those organs in particular. That was then forced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if -- forgive me, Mr. Vlaski. If not a single decision regarding staffing policies in the SRBH MUP will be implemented without the approval of Deputy Minister Momcilo Mandic, how is that going to aid cooperation and, as it were, make for a functioning joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It would help quite a lot, because these are the structures representing the SDA and the HDZ in that MUP made appointments however they wanted. They never asked anybody for anything. They did -- behaved according to their own conscience, which they didn't have. And they did what they wanted, and I am an example of that. They played with me, humiliated me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Conclusion number 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go over, please, to the next page, please, in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Work intensively to train and arm our police personnel." By "our," who did -- what was meant?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Parallel with this administrative and cadre policy, this other type of policy in the MUP was conducted to the detriment of the Serbian people. A vast imbalance was created in the distribution of the key positions as far as cadre reputation was concerned, as well as a de-balance in the reserve forces of the police in the arming of members of the police, in the procurement and distribution of weapons according to organisational units. The MUP was such that all the key functions were controlled by representatives of the Muslim and the Croatian people. The materiel financial service was under the control of Bruno Soco, and the minister was the responsible person who approved the funds for salaries and the functioning -- actually for the purchase of equipment and weaponry. This weaponry was not sent to the centres where the Serbs held the top positions or where the majority. No, quite the opposite. They were withdrawn if there. This is what happened with the equipment from the state security, which was withdrawn before any of the events, back to the seat in Sarajevo, from where anything could be done. And it could be manipulated according to the needs of those who were doing it, and these were done by chiefs, or colleagues among the Muslim and Croat people's ranks. This was done in order to create elementary conditions for a reserve police of Serbian ethnicity so that they would be able to carry out their assignments which were primarily quite certain, because of the increasing complexity of this political situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the simple answer to my question, "our," was this is to arm the reserve police of Serbian ethnicity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't see anyone else who would have to be armed. Those who wanted to go to the military responded to the call-up and they went to the army, and they had weapons there. I'm thinking of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That's all that I want to ask you about that meeting. Now, was there any other meetings that you attended after this meeting of the 11th of February that involved only Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I don't recall such a meeting being organised like this one in Banja Luka. I don't remember. Perhaps there was some contacts or talks, but a meeting of the type of a meeting, I do not recall taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any kind of meeting, however informal, that was held in Pale? Did you attend anywhere any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: It could happen that I did not, because, like I said, these others were more suitable to be invited to such a thing. I assume that I wasn't invited, but I don't allow the possibility that I didn't attend such a meeting, but I don't know when it was, who could have possibly attended it, or what could have been discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any meetings that you can recall where Mico Stanisic, Dragan Kijac, Milan Scekic, people like that, attended?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I know the people, but I don't remember them ever being in one place. There should have been some sort of reason for that, something that would link me or connect me with those people or that topic that would be the topic of such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, please, now, to the barricades incident at the beginning of March in Sarajevo. First, how did you first hear about the barricades being erected in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I heard on Sunday when I came back from skiing. I went to ski on Bjelasnica, and then, when I returned, I had a telephone call from Belgrade from a colleague who was in charge of security from Mr. Karadzic, and he was the first one who conveyed to me this information, because, at that time, I wasn't really following what was happening in the media, because, outside, I didn't have that possibility of getting to that information. I was informed about that event by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember which colleague informed you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Djordje Kapor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once you had been informed, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: After speaking with Mr. Kapor, there were calls probably to other members of the MUP, who were still working in the MUP at that time, for us to assemble in the premises of the designates or Deputies Club of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Djuro Djakovic Street. These are official premises used by parliamentarians, by deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Bosnian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I went. And there was a broadcast circle of people there who came because of this unfortunate incident in Sarajevo when the Serbian best man was killed in Bascarsija in the wedding party. And in view of the situation in the town, this required a kind of caution as far as personal, also in terms of the general situation which could arise from something like that. The gravity of the situation required that, other than the reaction that ensued along the political lines by the SDS, there had to be a certain reaction in the security sense by Serbian representatives of that same MUP which was then still a unified, single organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you pause there for a moment, please. You say the gravity of the political -- of the situation required something other than the reaction that ensued along political lines by the SDS. Why did this killing of a Serb guest at the wedding require a political reaction by the SDS, rather than just investigation by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Because the MUP did not wish to carry out a proper investigation into this because this was a classical political killing. It was not just a regular killing of the best man, something that can happen or any kind of killing which can happen in any town in the world. This was a political killing. And behind that killing stood the criminal structure which also had protection in the MUP, and this was something that was generally known. The majority of criminals were issued official identity cards by Minister Delimustafic, and they did not have to meet any regular institutional conditions for that. They would issue ID cards to criminals with criminal records so that they would do the bidding of individuals from the political structure. So this was something that we did not have a response to because the criminals had entered the ranks of the police. Those who fought against these people on the right side of the law were now colleagues with these people, and you could not expect an honest investigation. And this is why this kind of reaction followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You had as assistant minister, a Serb, Dr. Zepinic. Why couldn't it be left to him to deal with this, as opposed to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: He had the opportunity for a year, and this was valuable time lost, and there was nothing that had an effect to change the situation. He was also a professor, a intellectual who happened to fall into a situation where the upper hand was held by criminals. There was nothing much that he could do in such a situation. He could not come down to the level of the criminals with whom he had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I won't come along and list all the other Serb members in the MUP, but let's look at what happened at the beginning of March. When you got to the Deputies Club, you said a number of people were there. Who was there from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I didn't analyse that SDS composition much. I didn't know most of these people anyway. It was not relevant to me in that sense, who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's go through the people you did know. Was Dr. Karadzic there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: No, he was in Belgrade at that time, when this event occurred, and when the assembling began. He was in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was Velibor Ostojic there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I assume so, but I don't recall each individual who was present. Velibor was in the next phase of the development of the situation relating to the killing of this wedding party member. He was included in all the subsequent events because he was the minister for information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want you to cast your mind back, because you spoke about this during the interview, and tell who was there. Was Dr. Koljevic there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I cannot remember. They had a different position. The Presidency had its own area of work. I think perhaps he did drop by, but I really cannot remember. This was a very short time that we spent there. There was an assessment because of the new situation that that particular place was unfavorable from the security point of view, because there was a danger that members of this criminalised structure attacked this Deputies Club once they found out about the meeting, and then the decision was made to go to the Holiday Inn. That was a place, it's a hotel in Sarajevo where the majority of the foreign journalists were staying and the SDS did have - how to put it? - kind of position there because the director of the hotel was a director of Serb nationality and there was some sort of guarantee there that the -- there would be no problems. And that is why the meeting, namely all the activities in relation to this particular event, were then relocated to the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's deal who was at the Holiday Inn rather than at the Deputies Club? So let's start again, shall we? Who of the SDS was at the Holiday Inn when you all moved there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Mr. Rajko Dukic was there who was president of the SDS executive board. This is one of the more prominent figures both in the business and political life. And he was there since he had some kind of business arrangement in that hotel in that area, something like that, so he was in the function of the coordinating these activities of the SDS. That was Rajko Dukic. Velibor Ostojic, the minister of information was there, and many others. I really didn't have any ambitions to register them in that sort of sense. And as per their functions, probably there were many people because it was a hotel that anybody could enter who wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. But this was meeting, was it not, which was attended by members of the SDS according to you and also Serbian members of the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That is correct, because that is a place where people from the field would come. It was very busy just like a bus or a railway station. It wasn't a meeting where you could start it at 1500 hours an end at 1700 hours. The event of such a nature that it was an activity in continuity where people and events followed one another, then coordination occurred in some political and security aspects, and other aspects of this event. In the political sense, this was coordinated by Mr. Dukic who formulated the conclusions; the media aspect was along his line, as much as he could, was done by Mr. Velibor Ostojic. And as far as the security aspect, because the police, by the very nature of their work, had to carry on with the implementation of the regular tasks in the town. This required the police to take up some actions, so this required some sort of coordination of the police forces, including the police forces of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic was there, Kijac, Momo Mandic, I was there, Devedlaka, Goran Radovic, there were probably some others, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was any attempt made by you or by Mr. Stanisic or by anybody to make any planning to take down these barricades?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The barricades were organised in some parts of the city of Sarajevo by members of those local communities on their own initiative. Somewhere there was some coordination along the SDS lines because the party had its own infrastructure in the field and communication with their people in the field, and this was a spontaneous reaction, after the killing of the Serbian best man. This was a cry of the Serbs of Sarajevo that things could not could not go on anymore. Now this was a -- the last drop. There had been a killing, so this was a warning and a call of what we others could expect. So it was normal that it was necessary to seek a political reaction. And you can see that from what was formulated by the SDS, the political reply. Then the security response was the barricade, a barricade in itself means a blockade of some area or space in order to prevent something happening that you did not want to happen. This was just done by people. This was done along some sort of coordination of the SDS. I was not coordinating along that particular line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just ask you there to look briefly for the last couple of minutes at one document, which is the interview with Mr. Mandic that took place in Slobodna Bosna, 10th of April, and I believe it is it already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P735. And can we have, please, in the English the fourth page, and in the B/C/S, it's the - one, two, three - also the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to see this before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Mr. Mandic is being asked by the reporter about the barricades being organised by the SDS. And at the bottom of the paragraph he says: "Rajko Dukic headed the committee for the organisation of barricades. I do not wish to hide anything. Dragan Kijac, Mico Stanisic, and myself and some others from the MUP took part in this, and we organised everything so as to avoid bloodshed." First of all, was Dragan Kijac one of the people who you saw at the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you one of the committee for the organisation of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I was there, but I wasn't a member of any committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours, that I ask today, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, your testimony is not at an end. You're required to return tomorrow morning at 2.15 -- tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 when we will continue your testimony. Your examination-in-chief still has a -- a little while to go, and after which you would be -- counsel for the accused will be invited to cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have an hour and a half left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'm going to need anything like that -- well, depending on the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the -- sorry, Mr. Vlaski, I am obliged to remind you that, having been sworn as a witness, you can't have any communication with counsel from either side. And in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the courtroom, you can't discuss your testimony. So with that warning, we take the adjournment to tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
